claims.text: Single-phase CoCrFeMnNi exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior under ultra-high vacuum.
Dynamic amorphization governs hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Dynamic amorphization forms an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
Below a critical grain size, the near-surface layer increases resistance to plastic deformation through grain-boundary-mediated processes.
The near-surface layer gives rise to inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
CoCrFeMnNi can be studied as a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The coarse-grained initial material is comparatively soft.
Severe plastic deformation and controlled annealing can produce grain sizes below the threshold for dynamic amorphization.
Testing in an inert or ultra-high-vacuum environment mitigates oxidation and oxide-film effects.
The near-surface structure contains ultra-nanocrystalline material and high-angle grain boundaries.
The near-surface structure modifies shear strength and hardness.
Dynamic amorphization impedes dislocation motion and thereby enhances strength.
A dynamic-amorphization model predicts grain-size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime.
Ultrafine-grained samples will have greater hardness than coarse-grained samples.
Ultrafine-grained samples will have greater tensile strength than coarse-grained samples.
Reduced grain size and emergence of the amorphized layer will correlate with enhanced mechanical properties until grain-boundary stability becomes limiting.
The proposed behavior should extend to high-entropy alloys with compositions similar to CoCrFeMnNi.
Oxidizing environments may prevent the proposed behavior from applying.
Alloy chemistry or grain-boundary energies can preclude dynamic amorphization.
A post-deformation heat treatment can selectively disrupt or coarsen the near-surface amorphous layer.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes inverse Hall-Petch behavior below a critical grain size, but the mechanism and prediction state that further grain refinement impedes plasticity and increases hardness and strength. That direction is characteristic of conventional Hall-Petch strengthening rather than inverse Hall-Petch softening.

The same layer is described as amorphous and as ultra-nanocrystalline with high-angle grain boundaries. A fully amorphous phase has no grains or grain boundaries, so the structural state is not defined consistently.

The conditions state that grain size and associated near-surface microstructure are the only variables, whereas the falsification comparison adds a post-deformation heat treatment. That treatment can also alter bulk grain size, residual stress, defects, segregation, and phases, so the proposed control is not cleanly matched.

The falsification rule requires the intact, finer-layer condition to be stronger, while also requiring inverse Hall-Petch behavior. These criteria can demand opposite grain-size trends and therefore do not define one internally consistent decisive outcome.
